title: Who Finishes the Job? Fixing AI agents' code after the merge
topic: AI agents in real software projects

sources.title: Who Finishes the Job? A Study of Follow-Up Fixes and Commit Authorship on AI Coding Agent Pull Requests
sources.authors: Wannita Takerngsaksiri, Nhat Duong, Scott Barnett

summary_md:
**In one sentence:** a 2026 study followed thousands of AI-written code changes *after* they were accepted into
popular open-source projects and found that they need a confirmed fix more often than human changes (**1.62 times the
odds**), but that the agent that wrote a change usually fixes it itself (**69.6%** of the time).

### The basic words
- **Open-source project:** software whose code is public, so anyone can read it and suggest improvements (often on **GitHub**).
- **Commit:** one saved step of work: which lines changed, and who changed them.
- **Pull request (PR):** a bundle of commits offered to a project as one proposed change, which others can review.
- **Merged:** the project accepted the pull request, so the change is now part of the software.
- **AI coding agent:** an AI system that does a whole programming task and opens the pull request itself (here OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, Devin, Cursor and Claude Code).

### The problem
A merged agent PR is usually counted as finished work. But an accepted change can still be wrong, and then someone
must send a **follow-up fix**. Nobody had measured how often this happens for agents, or *who* does the fixing.

### What the researchers did
Takerngsaksiri, Duong and Barnett (Deakin University, Melbourne) took **6,774 merged agent PRs** from GitHub projects
with at least **500 stars**, plus **5,044 merged human PRs** from the same projects as a baseline. A filter found
*candidate* fixes (a later fix-type PR in the same project, within **30 days**, touching the same files). Two researchers
checked 50 pairs and agreed on 45; an **LLM judge** (an AI model used as a grader) labelled the rest, and was right
**90%** of the times it said "real fix".

*Analogy:* a builder (the agent) finishes a wall and the owner signs it off. How often does someone return within a
month to repair it, and is it the same builder?

### Key results
- **22.9%** of agent PRs had a candidate fix within 30 days, but only **4.5%** a verified one.
- Same projects, same period: **3.68%** of agent PRs vs **2.34%** of human PRs got a verified fix (odds ratio **1.62**).
- Fixes come fast: **half** of the 30-day fixes arrive in the **first week**.
- Who fixed agent work (263 fixes): the **same agent 69.6%**, a human **27.4%**, another agent **3.0%**. Human PRs were fixed by humans **89.1%** of the time.
- Inside agent fixes, on average **87.4%** of commits were agent-made (Codex excluded: it does not label its commits).
- At merge time, PRs that later needed a fix looked almost the same as the others. Within a project, a PR that took
  **10 times as many commits** had **6.1 times** the odds of a verified fix.

### Why it matters, and the limits
The merge is not the end of the job: AI work must be followed after it is accepted, and reviewers need to read the code,
not just the numbers around it. If an agent writes and fixes its own code, no human "insider" learns that code. The study
covers only five agents in popular projects and misses fixes after 30 days or in other files, so the real rates are
probably minimums. It measures who *wrote* a fix, not who reviewed it or is responsible for it.

### IELTS angle
Useful words: *premature*, *a point of comparison*, *modest but revealing*, *far from trivial*, *a mirror image*,
*there is no substitute for*. In Task 2, this study is a concrete example that "finished" AI work still
needs checking, and that credit and blame are harder to assign when machines do part of a job.

discussion: When a machine does part of a job, who do you think should be praised if the result is excellent?
Why might people trust work too quickly once it has been approved by a manager or an expert?
Do you think companies should tell customers when a product or service was partly made by AI? Why?

parts.title: Who Finishes the Job?
parts.passage_html:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1-14, which are based on the Reading Passage below.

A AI coding agents such as OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, Devin, Cursor and Claude Code no longer merely suggest the next few words of code: they can take on a whole task by themselves and submit the result to a real software project. Many of these contributions go to open-source projects, whose code is published so that anyone can read it and propose improvements. When a project accepts a contribution, it is said to be merged, and in most discussions of AI productivity that moment is treated as the finish line. This assumption, I would argue, is premature: a change that has been accepted can still turn out to be faulty, and somebody then has to come back and repair it.

B Programmers save their work in small recorded steps called commits, each of which notes exactly which lines were added or removed and who made the change. A group of commits that is offered to a project as a single proposal is known as a pull request, which others may review before it is merged. In a 2026 study, Wannita Takerngsaksiri, Nhat Duong and Scott Barnett of Deakin University in Melbourne followed 6,774 merged pull requests written by the five agents named above. All came from projects on GitHub, the leading code-sharing website, that had received at least 500 stars, a form of public approval similar to a 'like'. As a point of comparison, the researchers also collected 5,044 merged pull requests written by people in the same projects.

C The first challenge was to decide what counts as a repair. The team began with a broad filter: a later pull request counted as a candidate fix if it was merged into the same project within 30 days, was labelled as a fix, and changed at least one of the same files. Many candidates, however, simply extended or tidied earlier work rather than correcting a mistake. Two of the authors therefore examined 50 candidate pairs independently and agreed on 45 of them. These agreed examples were used to build an AI judge, a large language model that then labelled thousands of further pairs, and its decisions were later checked against fresh human judgements. When the judge declared that a change was a genuine fix, it was right nine times out of ten. To my mind, this careful verification is the most impressive feature of the study, because a filter alone would have counted many harmless changes as repairs.

D The headline figures are modest but revealing. Within 30 days, 22.9 per cent of merged agent pull requests attracted a candidate fix, but only 4.5 per cent were followed by a confirmed one. The more telling comparison is with human work: over a shared time window, 3.68 per cent of agent changes needed a confirmed fix, against 2.34 per cent of human ones, and when changes were compared only within the same projects, the agents' work had about 1.6 times the odds of needing repair. The problems also surfaced quickly: half of the fixes that appeared within a month had already arrived by the end of the first week. Four or five faulty changes in a hundred may not sound alarming, yet with nearly a million agent pull requests on GitHub in 2025 alone, the extra repair work is far from trivial.

E Perhaps the most surprising result concerns who did the repairing. Of the 263 confirmed fixes to agent work, 69.6 per cent were submitted by the very agent that had written the original change, 27.4 per cent by a human and only 3.0 per cent by a different agent. The pattern varied between products: GitHub Copilot fixed about 95 per cent of its own faulty changes, whereas people repaired 38.4 per cent of those made by OpenAI Codex. Human work showed a mirror image, with 89.1 per cent of fixes to human changes made by humans. Inside these repairs, on average 87.4 per cent of the commits in each agent fix were made by an agent, and 76.4 per cent of the fixes were entirely agent-written (Codex, which does not label its commits, was excluded).

F Could the faulty changes have been spotted before they were accepted? The researchers compared several measurements available at the moment of merging, such as the time spent under review and the amount of reviewer feedback. Across the whole sample, changes that later needed fixing looked almost identical to those that did not. Within individual projects, however, one signal stood out: a pull request that had needed ten times as many commits before acceptance had 6.1 times the odds of requiring a confirmed fix afterwards. In other words, work that was hard to finish before the merge tended to need more work after it. The lesson, I believe, is that reviewers cannot rely on such surface statistics to protect them; there is no substitute for actually reading the code.

G The study has clear limits, which the authors acknowledge. It covers only five agents in popular projects, and its method misses repairs that arrive after 30 days or alter different files, so the true rates of fixing may well be higher than those reported. It also leaves open a larger question of ownership. In human teams, abandoned code is usually adopted by experienced colleagues who know its history; an agent that writes and repairs its own work leaves no such insider behind, and nobody yet knows what will happen to its code once the model responsible is withdrawn. The finding that agents largely clean up after themselves is therefore only partly reassuring. What it shows beyond doubt is that a merge is no longer the end of the job.

writing.prompt:
Artificial intelligence now often completes part of a task, such as writing a report or a piece of software, which a person then checks and submits. Some people believe that the person who submits the work should receive all the credit and take full responsibility for any mistakes. Others think that the credit and the responsibility should be shared with the companies that make the AI tools.

Discuss both these views and give your own opinion.

The chart below shows who made the confirmed follow-up fixes to changes that had been accepted into popular open-source software projects in 2024-2025, according to who wrote the original change.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
writing.image_description: Grouped bar chart, percentage of confirmed follow-up fixes made by each type of fixer, by author of the original accepted change (popular open-source projects, 2024-2025). Values given as the same agent / a human / another AI agent or bot: OpenAI Codex 59.2 / 38.4 / 2.4; Devin 72.7 / 23.9 / 3.4; GitHub Copilot 95.0 / 5.0 / 0.0; All AI agents 69.6 / 27.4 / 3.0; Human authors: same agent not applicable, a human 89.1, another AI agent or bot 10.9. Main trends: for every agent most fixes came from the same agent that wrote the change, ranging from 59.2% (Codex) to 95% (Copilot); humans fixed a large share of Codex's changes (38.4%) but almost none of Copilot's (5%); fixes by a different agent were rare (0-3.4%). Changes written by humans were overwhelmingly fixed by humans (89.1%), a mirror image of the agents' self-fixing (69.6% overall).
